note: Things people say at a trading counter or a camp (ASK FOR NEWS), in their own words. Information only: no rule reads this file, so it is not part of the rules fingerprint.
sources: Joseph Meek reached St. Joseph on 4 May 1848 with word of the Whitman killings (Oregon Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, Joseph Meek).
The ship Honolulu reached Portland in summer 1848, buying tools with California gold dust (Offbeat Oregon, H023).
Paris revolution news was in New York by late March 1848 (Michigan Liberty Press, 13 April 1848).
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo: signed 2 February, ratified by the Senate 10 March, proclaimed 4 July 1848. Oregon Territory Act signed 14 August 1848.
Road notes follow Joel Palmer's 1847 journal and NPS Oregon Trail narratives already cited in route.json.

headlines.text: Last we heard, General Scott's got Mexico City, and they're dickering over a peace.
The Senate passed the peace treaty with Mexico. We get California and New Mexico for fifteen million dollars, if you can believe it.
Did you hear about France? They've run King Louis Philippe out of Paris and made it a republic again. The papers say it's spreading all over Europe.

Joe Meek came through on his way to Washington. He says the Cayuse killed Dr. Whitman and his wife at their mission last November, and a dozen more with them. Oregon's raised volunteers to fight them.
Colonel Gilliam's dead. He was leading the Oregon volunteers and shot himself by accident in camp. They've built a fort where the Whitman mission burned.
The Democrats met in Baltimore and picked Lewis Cass of Michigan for President.
Wisconsin's a state now. That makes thirty.
Brigham Young's bringing the whole body of the Mormons out to the Salt Lake this year. They keep to the north side of the Platte, so you won't run into them much.
The army's sent soldiers to build a fort at the head of Grand Island. A Lieutenant Woodbury is in charge of it.
The Whigs have nominated Old Rough and Ready, General Taylor, the one who won at Buena Vista.
A man from the Salt Lake says crickets came down on the Mormon wheat this spring, and the gulls flew in and ate them. The Mormons are calling it a miracle.
Peace with Mexico was proclaimed on the Fourth of July. The boys are coming home.
Most of the Oregon volunteers have gone back to their farms. A few are still holding the Whitman place, and they never did catch the Cayuse who did the killing.

A ship came up the Columbia and bought every pick and shovel in Portland, and paid for them in gold dust. They say gold's lying loose in the creeks down in California. Half of Oregon's talking about going.
There's a new party now, the Free Soil men. They met in Buffalo and put up Martin Van Buren again. They don't want slavery in the new territories.
Congress finally made Oregon a territory, and slavery's barred there. Now they'll send out a governor from Washington.
The New York papers are printing letters about gold on the American River in California. Most folks back home think it's a tall tale.
General Taylor's won it. He'll be the next President.

road.elm_grove: There's nothing left at Elm Grove but a stump or two. Everybody's cut the trees for firewood, so bring your own from the last creek.
road.wakarusa: The Wakarusa's got steep banks. You'll have to let the wagons down with ropes.
road.kansas_river: You can't ford the Kansas most of the year. There's ferrymen who'll take you across, for a price.
road.big_vermilion: The Vermilion's got steep clay banks, but there's wood and good water. Most trains lay over a day there.
road.big_blue: Watch the Big Blue. It comes up fast after a rain, and I've seen trains wait days for it to go down.
road.little_blue: Up the Little Blue the camps are good for days, timber and grass both. Enjoy it while it lasts.
road.platte: Once you hit the Platte, it's flat going for weeks. There's hardly any wood, though, so you'll be burning buffalo chips.
road.fort_kearny: There's soldiers camped at the head of Grand Island this summer, but don't expect a store there yet.
road.south_platte: The South Platte's wide and shallow, but the bottom's quicksand. Keep your teams moving or the wheels will sink.
road.ash_hollow: The hill down into Ash Hollow is a terror. Lock the wheels and rope the wagons down. There's good spring water and wood at the bottom, though.
road.courthouse_rock: You'll see Courthouse Rock off to the south. It looks a lot closer than it is, so don't go walking out to it.
road.chimney_rock: You'll be looking at Chimney Rock for two or three days before you get to it.
road.scotts_bluff: The road swings south around the bluffs, away from the river. Water's scarce through there.
road.fort_laramie: Fort Laramie's an American Fur Company post. Their prices are steep, and plenty of folks throw out what they can't haul there, before the hills.
road.horseshoe_creek: Past Laramie the road goes up over the Black Hills. Horse Shoe Creek's the first good camp, clear water and timber.
road.deer_creek: Deer Creek's the best camp this side of the mountains. Grass, cottonwood, and you can catch fish there.
road.north_platte: The Mormons run a ferry at the upper crossing of the North Platte. I wouldn't try to ford it if the water's up.
road.willow_spring: Don't camp at the mineral springs after the crossing. Push on to Willow Spring; the water's cold and sweet there.
road.independence_rock: Don't let your cattle drink from the springs between the Platte and the Sweetwater. They're alkali, and they'll kill an ox.
road.devils_gate: The Sweetwater cuts right through the rock at Devil's Gate. The road goes around it.
road.south_pass: South Pass is so gentle you'll hardly notice you've crossed the top. The nights are cold up there, even in July.
road.little_sandy: After Pacific Springs it's dry country. Fill every keg and canteen you've got.
road.green_river: The Green's fast and deep. There's ferrymen at the southern crossing, and they charge more when the river's up.
road.greenwood_cutoff: Greenwood's Cutoff saves you some days, but it's about forty miles with no water. Travel at night and carry water and grass with you.
road.fort_bridger: Bridger and Vasquez keep a little post with a blacksmith. You won't find much to buy there.
road.salt_lake: The Mormons have a city in the valley past Bridger's now. They've had a hungry year with the crickets, so don't count on buying flour there.
road.bear_river: Where the Bridger road meets the cutoff on Bear River there's good grass and willows. Big Hill's just beyond, and it's a pull.
road.soda_springs: At Soda Springs the water bubbles right up out of the ground and tastes like soda. It's good drinking.
road.fort_hall: Fort Hall belongs to the Hudson's Bay Company. They've got flour, but it'll cost you.
road.american_falls: Below Fort Hall the Snake falls over a ledge of black rock. The Snake Indians fish there.
road.raft_river: At the Raft River the California road turns off south. Mind you don't follow the wrong wheel tracks, unless you mean to take the Applegates' South Road, and that's a long, hungry way round.
road.salmon_falls: At Salmon Falls the Indians will trade you dried salmon for powder or an old shirt. It's the best eating you'll get along the Snake.
road.snake_river: Along the Snake the road stays up above the canyon, and half the time you can't get down to the water. The grass is poor too.
road.fort_boise: Fort Boise is just a little Hudson's Bay post. You cross the Snake again near there, and it's a deep ford.
road.malheur: There's hot springs at the Malheur. You can boil your coffee in them, near enough.
road.burnt_river: The Burnt River canyon is the worst road yet. You'll be crossing that creek all day long.
road.powder_river: There's fair grass along the Powder. Rest your teams there if you can.
road.grande_ronde: The Grande Ronde is a fine valley, good grass and water. Rest your animals there before the Blue Mountains.
road.blue_mountains: The road over the Blue Mountains is steep and thick with timber. Snow can come by the end of September.
road.umatilla: The road comes down to the Umatilla. It's been unsettled since the Whitman killings, so travel with other wagons.
road.umatilla_mouth: Where the Umatilla comes into the Columbia the Walla Walla road joins in. It's sand and wind from there.
road.fort_walla_walla: The Hudson's Bay men at Walla Walla are staying out of the war. The Oregon volunteers are holding the burned mission at Waiilatpu.
road.john_day: Along the Columbia it's all sand and rock, and there's hardly any grass.
road.deschutes: The Indians at the Deschutes will ferry your goods across in canoes, for pay. You'll have to swim the stock over.
road.the_dalles: At The Dalles you've got to choose: the Barlow Road over the Cascades, and they charge a toll, or rafting down the Columbia.
road.columbia_raft: Nobody runs the Cascades of the Columbia. You'll have to carry everything around them.
road.barlow_pass: The Barlow Road climbs through heavy timber south of Mount Hood. Cut grass for your stock wherever you find it.
road.laurel_hill: Laurel Hill's so steep they let the wagons down on ropes wrapped around the trees.
road.eagle_creek: Philip Foster's got a farm at Eagle Creek. He sells flour and beef to folks coming off the Barlow Road.
road.city_of_rocks: Past the Raft River the California road goes by a city of rocks, tall as churches. The Oregon men who take the South Road go that way too, as far as the Humboldt.
road.humboldt_wells: Mary's River starts at some deep springs in a meadow. Follow it down and it gets worse every week: bad water, poor grass, and Paiutes shooting arrows into the cattle at night.
road.gravelly_ford: There's a gravel ford on the Humboldt about halfway down. Keep a guard on your stock every night along there, or you'll find them stuck full of arrows.
road.lassen_meadows: Where the Applegate road leaves the Humboldt, fill every keg you've got. It's two days and more of desert to the Black Rock, and the springs on the way are poor.
road.black_rock: At the Black Rock there's springs hot enough to scald a dog. Let the water cool before the stock gets at it.
road.high_rock_canyon: High Rock Canyon has grass and water, but the walls are close. I'd not camp under them without a guard out.
road.fandango_pass: The pass into the Goose Lake country is steep as a roof on the far side. You'll want ropes to let the wagons down.
road.goose_lake: A company lost a good part of their cattle to raiders by Goose Lake last year. Keep your stock close in.
road.tule_lake: There's a stone bridge over the Lost River past the big tule lake. The Modocs there don't care for wagons coming through.
road.klamath_river: The Klamath's fordable on a rock ledge in the fall. After that it's timber and mountains till the Rogue.
road.green_springs: Over the Cascade summit by the Green Springs it's steep going down, and snow comes early up there.
road.rogue_valley: The Rogue River valley is the prettiest country on the South Road, but the Rogue River people shot horses in a camp there last fall. Keep together.
road.canyon_creek: Don't let the rains catch you in the Umpqua canyon. Two years back folks left their wagons in the creek and walked out with what they could carry.
road.umpqua_valley: Once you're out of the canyon the Umpqua country's easy, and the Indians there will trade you salmon.
road.south_willamette: From the head of the Willamette it's a week or so of easy road down the valley to Oregon City.
road.oregon_city: Oregon City's at the falls of the Willamette. Food's dear there since the war.
